comments.author: @aremoreequal
comments.text: Human beings have dealt with similar problems before. One such problem is named, "Buffer Overload," and people would do buffer overload attacks. I think the short-term obvious solution is to filter out these otherwise unused Unicode characters before giving the data onto the LLM (in most cases). Once a Unicode actually becomes used for something besides encoding secret messages, then we add that one into the the characters that can get through the filter. - I don't fully understand the Unicode thing, but I still feel like protecting the LLMs a similar way to how we protect username and password boxes on websites against buffer overload or overflow attacks would solve this problem.

Not sure why he mentioned “confusables” which are called homoglyphs, as they don’t pose any real threat as an LLM sees them for what they are and not what they look like when rendered, but this is less of a hack and more about OpenAI not doing basic string scrubbing on their training data.

They really should have Justus removed non printable Unicode characters from regular training data and done specific training data so the model is aware of them and what they are.

Anyone who has had to do text moderation or sanitization knows you need to handle these chars in a thought out way. I steady they got lazy and opened up some potential vulnerabilities.

comments.text: 4:43 For the 'g' example, you could have a font that has a g that looks like the two rings joined together, and another choice that looks like one ring and an open ring connected below it, and the variation selector is how you choose which one shows.  This is exposed in high-end typesetting software like Adobe InDesign, and ignored in most text-editing software.  It is common to have 4 different designs for numerals:  They can be proportional or monospaced, and they can be the modern style (which is all caps) or the old style of straddling the baseline (that is, a 9 looks more like a lower-case 'g').

> I’m experimenting with a symbolic control layer for LLMs that replaces natural language with a finite set of operational emojis, each mapped to a deterministic function.

The result is a protocol where the LLM acts like a state machine:
– no ambiguity,
– no natural-language re-interpretation,
– no prompt injection via hidden bytes,
– no jailbreaks.

Because emojis are atomic Unicode units (not composable byte sequences), the model cannot be misled by invisible variation selectors, homoglyphs, or multi-byte fuzzing.

The system forces the model to follow a strict grammar:
EMOJI → MODE → OUTPUT SHAPE.

It works across GPT, Claude, Copilot, etc.
The protocol is called NurJana Emoji Protocol — an operational language for AI that behaves consistently, predictably, and securely.

If you’re interested, I can share the evaluation steps and failure-mode analysis.

The thing is, none of this is good. AI has never been secure and we are learning all the time that its less secure than we thought it was.
Think of it from the perspective of Musk who is currently stealing really sensitive data from the people of the US and when that model leaks, it's going to be really easy to access that data because AI is insecure.

There should have been a pause on AI ages ago because it's just not ready for what it is currently being used for.
Another issue is AI still has and will always have a hallucination problem and I'm now seeing people in debates using the generated response from AI as if it was 100% correct fact. 
Which is so stupid, nobody should be trusting the generated response from an AI, you must check everything it tells you, it will lie to you (meaning the data might have errors).

One last thing is non-programmers keep telling everybody how amazing AI is because it's getting better with each version and "What will it be like in the future?".
What they are not understanding is, it's not getting better, it's just getting less things wrong, but it's still getting a ton of things wrong.

A way to think of it is like imagine driving a car down a road and the road is full of obstacles that shouldn't have been there.
Each new version of the AI is like that road having less obstacles in the way.
The road itself hasn't actually got any better, it's just removed things that shouldn't have been there, which gives the illusion that it's better.

People should be angry that the road is full of obstacles, instead they are amazed that the car hit less obstacles in the new model.
It's pretty crazy.
